moduleTitle: Sanctity of life, abortion and euthanasia

note.specFocus: Christian teaching on the value of human life and differing Christian and non-religious attitudes to abortion and euthanasia.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
2.3 Sanctity of Life, Abortion and Euthanasia
Sanctity of life is the belief that human life is sacred and has inherent value because it is a gift from God, which shapes Christian views on abortion and euthanasia.
Sanctity of life
• Genesis 1:27: humans are made "in the image of God" (imago Dei), giving every person inherent worth regardless of ability, age or health.
• Exodus 20:13, "You shall not murder", is widely used to argue that only God has authority over when human life begins and ends.
Abortion
• Most Christian denominations, especially the Catholic Church, teach that life begins at conception, so abortion is viewed as ending an innocent human life and is generally opposed, except in rare cases to save the mother's life.
• Some more liberal Christians weigh the sanctity of the foetus's life against compassion for the mother's circumstances, arguing that abortion may sometimes be, in Joseph Fletcher's situation-ethics terms, "the most loving thing to do".
• Non-religious views on abortion often emphasise the woman's right to choose (bodily autonomy) over the moral status of the foetus.
Euthanasia
• Most Christians oppose euthanasia, citing Job 1:21 ("the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away") to argue that only God should decide when life ends.
• The hospice movement, pioneered by the Christian Dame Cicely Saunders, is often presented by Christians as a compassionate alternative that manages pain and suffering without ending life.
• Supporters of legal euthanasia emphasise personal autonomy and compassion for unbearable suffering, especially in terminal illness.
Exam link: keep abortion and euthanasia arguments separate even though both relate to sanctity of life — questions will usually specify which issue to address.

questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. Genesis 1:27 teaches that human beings are made "in the image of God" (imago Dei), which most Christians believe gives every human life inherent, sacred value that must be respected and protected.

2. The commandment "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13) is widely used by Christians to argue that human life belongs ultimately to God, so people do not have an unrestricted right to end innocent human life, including at its beginning or end.
questions.question: Choose one religion. Outline two teachings about the sanctity of life in this religion.

questions.examTip: For a 12-mark evaluation, use accurate religious teaching, explain different religious or non-religious views, analyse the statement and reach a justified conclusion. The conclusion should follow from the arguments you have discussed.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Situation ethics, developed by the Christian thinker Joseph Fletcher, argues that the most loving thing to do should guide moral decisions; some use this to argue that helping a suffering person to die peacefully, at their own request, can be the most compassionate choice.

A second consideration is: Supporters of legalisation also appeal to personal autonomy: individuals should have the right to make decisions about the ending of their own suffering, especially in cases of terminal illness with no hope of recovery.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Most Christian denominations, including the Catholic Church, teach that only God has the right to give and take life (Job 1:21, "the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away"), so euthanasia is viewed as a form of killing that undermines the sanctity of life.

A further consideration is: Opponents also raise the "slippery slope" argument, fearing that legal euthanasia could pressure vulnerable, elderly or disabled people to end their lives; many Christians instead point to hospice care, pioneered by the Christian Dame Cicely Saunders, as a compassionate alternative that manages suffering without ending life.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: supporters prioritise compassion and personal choice in the face of suffering, while most Christian teaching prioritises the sanctity of life and trusts God, alongside palliative care, with the timing and manner of death. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.

questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of imago Dei, sanctity of life, compassion, quality of life and the principle of double effect and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
